det_01.label: The Pudding's 'Lady-O' study (origin)
det_01.content: This dataset was assembled by Jada Watson (a music industry researcher who runs SongData) and Jan Diehm of The Pudding for an article published May 2023 titled 'They Won't Play a Lady-O on Country Radio: Examining Back-to-Back Plays by Gender, Race, and Sexual Orientation.' The team pulled 24-hour Mediabase logs from 29 large-market country radio stations, selecting 19 dates across 2022 — 12 month-end Fridays plus 7 dates that aligned with new releases by women artists, to give female songs the best possible chance of being heard. Each song was hand-coded by gender, race, and sexual orientation, then a script flagged every consecutive same-category pair — a back-to-back — for analysis. The whole point was to test whether country radio's long-rumored 'don't play two women in a row' rule was real, programmatic, and measurable.

det_02.label: Tomato-gate: the rule is named out loud (2015)
det_02.content: In May 2015, country-radio consultant Keith Hill told the trade publication Country Aircheck that programmers should not schedule two women back-to-back. His exact analogy: 'Trust me, I play great female records, and we've got some right now; they're just not the lettuce in our salad. The lettuce is Luke Bryan and Blake Shelton, Keith Urban and artists like that. The tomatoes of our salad are the females.' The remark — quickly nicknamed 'Tomato-gate' or 'SaladGate' — was the first time an unwritten programming rule passed around in country radio for decades was stated publicly and on the record. Martina McBride called it 'sexist and condescending'; Miranda Lambert called it 'bullshit' on Twitter; Jennifer Nettles, Reba McEntire, and Carrie Underwood all spoke out. The Pudding's 2022 dataset is the first attempt to actually measure whether the rule kept being followed in the eight years after Hill said it.

det_03.label: Why women's airplay matters: the career-stack consequence
det_03.content: Country radio is not just one input among many — it is the gate that controls almost everything else. Airplay drives chart position; chart position drives label promotion budgets; promotion drives festival bookings, award eligibility (the CMAs, ACMs and Grammy country categories all weigh radio activity), and tour revenue. When women receive only 11% of airplay, every downstream system inherits that floor: smaller advances, fewer single releases, fewer label signings, fewer slots at the Opry and at country festivals. Brandi Carlile, in a widely cited interview tied to the Pudding piece, framed the stakes as generational: 'What does that say to a 10-year-old girl about life?' The point of measuring back-to-back rates is not curiosity — it is showing that the upstream constraint is still active.

det_04.label: The historical baseline: women's share of country radio over 50 years
det_04.content: Women's share of country radio is not at a normal-low; it is at a historical low. Watson's earlier SongData research, the 2019 'Gender Representation on Country Format Radio' report, traced women on the Billboard Country Airplay chart from 1969 to 2019 and found peaks of 33.1% in 1999 and a steady decline to 11.4% in 2015 — the year of Hill's 'tomato' quote. By 2022 it averaged roughly 15% but back-to-back women plays specifically remained around 0.5%. This long sweep matters because it shows the back-to-back rule is not the whole story: the share started shrinking before 2015 and continued shrinking after. Tomato-gate is a symptom, not the cause.

det_05.label: Race and queerness: a category of one
det_05.content: Watson's coding tracks not just gender but race and sexual orientation. The race and orientation findings are the rawest in the dataset. In 2022, only 0.03% of plays on the 156 Mediabase-tracked stations went to Black or biracial women. LGBTQ+ artists collectively received 0.13% of airplay and the entire 2022 dataset contains a single back-to-back queer pair across 182,848 songs. The historical layer makes this concrete: Linda Martell remains the highest-charting Black woman in country history, with a 1969 chart entry that has never been surpassed; Crystal Shawanda was the last Indigenous woman to chart, in 2008; Mickey Guyton, the last Black woman to chart, did so in 2016. Asian women have never received country radio airplay; non-binary and trans artists are absent from the format entirely.

det_06.label: Mickey Guyton's 'What Are You Gonna Tell Her' and 'Black Like Me'
det_06.content: Mickey Guyton's 2020 song 'What Are You Gonna Tell Her' was performed at the Country Radio Seminar to a 2,400-strong audience of programmers and on-air talent — the people who decide who gets played. The song asks what a parent says to a Black girl when she discovers the country format will not give her the same chances it gives her white male peers. Variety called it country music's song of the year. Guyton's follow-up 'Black Like Me' became a Grammy nomination and a flagship example of country radio's race problem: the song was widely celebrated by critics, and barely played on country radio. Her career is the human shape of the 0.03% statistic — when the data says 'Black women are not played,' it is saying the artists who would otherwise have been played are not Hill's hypothetical 'tomatoes' but Guyton, specifically.

det_07.label: Reverse roles: men's back-to-back rate as a benchmark
det_07.content: The Pudding piece reports that across the 29-station sample, songs by men were played back-to-back roughly 60-65% of the time. That is not a coincidence — it is the mathematical expectation of a format where ~80% of plays are by men. If a station played randomly with no avoidance, women's back-to-back rate would float around 1-2% (the square of women's airplay share). The Pudding's permutation test shuffled each station's 24-hour log 1,000 times, with no avoidance rule applied, and asked: how often do you see a women's back-to-back rate as low as the observed one? At 17 of 29 stations, the answer was 'less often than chance' — meaning the observed pattern is not just under-representation, it is under-representation plus active separation. The men's number is the ceiling that lets us see how floor-low the women's number is.

det_08.label: Daypart trick: women on the graveyard shift
det_08.content: When women are played, they are played when fewer people are listening. The Pudding piece reports that in 2022, 46.1% of women's back-to-back plays happened during overnights (midnight to 6 a.m.) and another 19% during evening hours (7 p.m. to midnight) — roughly 65% of women's back-to-backs concentrated in dayparts where listenership is at its weekly low. The morning drive (6-10 a.m. AMD) and afternoon drive (3-7 p.m. PMD), where ratings and ad revenue peak, are where men are stacked. This is the mechanism that makes the 11% airplay number even more punishing in practice: it is not 11% across the day, it is closer to 5% during the hours that count for ratings. Watson's broader work flags this as the practical translation of Hill's rule — women are not absent, they are quarantined.

det_09.label: Glossary: gold, recurrent, current
det_09.content: Country radio sorts every song into three programming buckets: 'current' (a recently released song actively being promoted), 'recurrent' (a song that just rotated off current and is still played for a few months), and 'gold' (an established hit, often years or decades old). These buckets matter because labels invest in promotion only when a song has a chance to chart — which means radio's behavior toward 'current' women's songs is the leading indicator of whether women still have a path. Watson's previous work, and the Pudding piece, both report that women's back-to-backs concentrate in 'gold' (older hits) rather than 'current' songs — meaning when a station does play two women in a row, it is usually a Reba McEntire/Faith Hill 'safe' pair, not two new artists in promotion. This is one reason the format keeps reproducing itself: new women never get the spin density needed to become the next safe gold pair five years from now.

det_10.label: The 'flip the roles' counterfactual
det_10.content: Watson and The Pudding ran a thought experiment as a sanity check: take each station's 24-hour log and swap every man's name with a woman's, holding everything else constant — the avoidance rule, the song-level slotting, the dayparting. The result is a hypothetical day where roughly 80% of slots are women. Even applying the same rule of 'don't play two women back-to-back' to that flipped log, women's back-to-backs would still appear at >25-30% of plays simply because there are not enough men to insert as separators. The actual observed women's back-to-back rate (~0.5%) is therefore impossible to produce without an active rule on top of the airplay-share imbalance. This is what 'systemic' means in the dataset: even after you account for the share, the gap is still bigger than chance.

det_11.label: Scope suggestion: what the analyst should focus on
det_11.content: The dataset's centre of gravity is the contrast between three numbers per station: women's airplay share, women's back-to-back share, and the same numbers from the men's column. The most informative analyses will (a) rank all 29 stations by women's back-to-back rate so the reader can see how thin the differences are, (b) compute the daypart distribution of women's plays so the 'graveyard shift' pattern is visible, (c) compute the gold/recurrent/current breakdown so the 'old hits only' pattern is visible, (d) compute the reverse-roles simulation per station so we can quantify how impossible the observed numbers would be without an active rule, and (e) extract the most extreme single station (the one that came closest to never playing two women back-to-back) as a concrete narrative anchor. The analyst should NOT try to reproduce the full 1000-iteration permutation test from scratch — the analysis directory already contains pvals.csv with those results, which can be loaded directly.

instances.label: Mickey Guyton — Black Like Me
instances.why: The single most-cited example of a celebrated Black woman's country song that radio refused to play in 2020. Listening to it directly grounds the 0.03% airplay figure for Black women.

instances.label: Lainey Wilson — Things A Man Oughta Know
instances.why: Wilson is one of the three contemporary women whose songs make up >50% of all current-women airplay in the 2022 dataset — the bottleneck is audible.

instances.label: Carrie Underwood — Before He Cheats
instances.why: An archetypal 'gold' women's song — released in 2005, still in heavy rotation in 2022. Most women's back-to-back plays consist of pairs like this with another classic.

instances.label: Reba McEntire — Fancy
instances.why: Another canonical 'gold' women's track — and Reba was one of the public voices against Tomato-gate in 2015.

instances.label: Maren Morris — The Bones
instances.why: Morris is one of the few post-2015 women to break through; lets the reader hear what 'breaking through' actually sounds like in this format.

instances.label: Linda Martell — Color Him Father
instances.why: 1969 single by the highest-charting Black woman in country music history; concretely anchors the half-century of erasure described in det_05.

instances.label: Morgan Wallen — Last Night
instances.why: The contrast point: 2023's biggest country hit by a man — the 'lettuce' that fills the playlists women are not stacked alongside.

instances.label: Luke Combs — Beautiful Crazy
instances.why: Another archetypal back-to-back-eligible men's track from 2018-19 still in 2022 rotation — useful as the men's mirror to 'Before He Cheats.'
